newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten says no evidence HK passport list leaked.
newsitem.headline: Patten says no evidence HK passport list leaked.

text.p: Governor Chris Patten on Thursday sought to allay fears that a sensitive list of Hong Kong citizens granted British passports had been leaked to China.

"I know of no evidence, I have no evidence that Chinese officials have lists of the possible beneficiaries under the BNS (British Nationality Scheme)," Patten told an emergency session of Hong Kong's Legislative Council.

Patten addressed the emergency session in an attempt to defuse a shock admission by British envoy Francis Cornish this week that Britain could not fully protect Hong Kong holders of British passports after China takes over the colony next year.

The furore is the latest to rock confidence in the British colony in the bumpy transition to Chinese rule 208 days from now, when 150 years of colonial rule ends and Hong Kong is handed back to China.
China regards the holders of British passports obtained under a special scheme as dual citizens and therefore not entitled to full consular protection.
A local newspaper quoted Chinese officials as saying Beijing claimed it would be able to track down those who had benefited from the scheme.
Questioned on the whereabouts of the detailed information provided by applicants, Patten said he could offer only a qualified answer and would provide a written answer later.
He said he understood the Hong Kong immigration department which administered the scheme was transferring the information to a British Consulate being set up ahead of the handover.
"I want to assure everybody in Hong Kong that we will do everything humanly and technologically possible to keep that material secure and to keep that information confidential," Patten said.

Earlier in the day, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai repeated Beijing's policy of not permitting British consular protection for holders of dual citizenship on the mainland or in Hong Kong, but sought to play down fears.
"Although a small number of people are concerned...I think (the concern) is unnecessary," he said.
Patten said Britain would continue to offer assistance, if not full consular protection to dual citizens in need.
British officials say British passports issued to about 135,000 Hong Kong people under a special scheme were indistinguishable from any other full British passport.
"A British passport obtained under the British Nationaity Scheme is the same as the passport I've got," Patten said, brandishing his burgundy passport before the chamber.

Britain offered passports to 50,000 Hong Kong households, a privileged fraction of the territory's 6.3 million people, in a concession to widespread demands for the insurance of full British citizenship in the wake of Beijing's 1989 crackdown on student-led protests in Tiananmen Square.

The transition to Chinese rule has been dogged by disputes since the Tiananmen crackdown. China reacted with fury to the special passport scheme, and again when Patten introduced reforms expanding democracy in 1992.
Relations took a downturn again last week Britain angered China by unveiling a liberal anti-subversion bill that would set legal markers against China-style jailings of dissidents in Hong Kong.

British and Chinese negotiators are in the midst of a three-day bargaining session on handover details and have signalled they expect to announce accords on several issues on Friday, although the agenda has so far remained confidential.
